statements.claim: A great solar eclipse occurs, and the Yadavas journey to Samanta-panchaka to bathe and give cows and gifts.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (BP 10.82.1-15): 'A great solar eclipse occurs, and the Yadavas, together with Vasudeva, Akrura and others, journey to Samanta-panchaka ... to bathe and give cows and gifts.'

statements.claim: Samanta-panchaka is the field of the Kurus where Rama, best of weapon-bearers, once made the earth free of the kings (made lakes of kings' blood).
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.2: 'niḥkṣatriyāṃ mahīṃ kurvan rāmaḥ śastra-bhṛtāṃ varaḥ' — Rama, best of weapon-bearers, making the earth free of kshatriyas; index: 'the field where Rama had once made lakes of the kings' blood'.

statements.claim: The blessed Rama hallowed the field with his great sacrifice, though untouched by any deed's stain.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.3: 'īje ca bhagavān rāmo yatrāspṛṣṭo 'pi karmaṇā' — Lord Rama performed the sacrifice there, untouched by karma.

statements.claim: Krishna went, with Balarama, Vasudeva, Akrura and the chief men of the Yadava houses.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'the Yadavas, together with Vasudeva, Akrura and others, journey to Samanta-panchaka'; BP 10.82.10: 'vṛṣṇayaḥ kṛṣṇa-devatāḥ' (the Vrishnis whose deity is Krishna).

statements.claim: The road filled with chariots gleaming like the dwellings of the gods, drawn by swift horses and hung with garlands of gold.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.6-7: 'te rathair deva-dhiṣṇyābhair hayaiś ca tarala-plavaiḥ / vyarocanta mahā-tejāḥ pathi kāñcana-mālinaḥ'.

statements.claim: It seemed all the people of the land were on the road, each hoping to leave his sins behind in the sacred water.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.4-5: 'mahatyāṃ tīrtha-yātrāyāṃ tatrāgan bhāratīḥ prajāḥ / yayur bhārata tat kṣetraṃ svam aghaṃ kṣapayiṣṇavaḥ' — Bharata's people came to that field to destroy their own sin.

statements.claim: At the tirtha they bathed in Rama's pools, fasting with minds gathered close, and then bathed a second time as the rite required; they gave cows and gifts.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.8-9: 'tatra snātvā mahā-bhāgā upoṣya su-samāhitāḥ / rāma-hradeṣu vidhi-vat punar āplutya vṛṣṇayaḥ'. The 'five pools' phrasing glosses the place-name Samanta-panchaka (the five lakes of Rama); the verse itself says 'Rama's pools' without the numeral.

statements.claim: Kings had come from Kamboja, Kaikaya, Madra, Kunti, Anarta and Kerala.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.12: 'kāmboja-kaikayān madrān kuntīn ānarta-keralān'.

statements.claim: Long-separated kinsmen embraced one another with joy, hearts and faces opening like lotuses, tears flowing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.13: 'anyonya-sandarśana-harṣa-raṃhasā protphulla-hṛd-vaktra-saroruha-śriyaḥ'; verse 11: 'suhṛt-sambandhino nṛpān'.

statements.claim: The women of the two houses embraced, kumkuma-marked, with tears of love in their eyes.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.14: 'striyaś ca ... kuṅkuma-paṅka-rūṣitān ... praṇayāśru-locanāḥ'. Story relocates the kumkuma mark from breasts (verse) to shoulders — a modest rendering of the same detail, not a contradiction.

statements.claim: The youngest saluted the elders and were blessed in return.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.15: 'tato 'bhivādya te vṛddhān yaviṣṭhair abhivāditāḥ'.

statements.claim: Toward the end of the day a caravan of cowherds arrived — Nanda, Yashoda and the cowherds of Gokula.
statements.evidence: Corpus-chain continuity with DKS_0492 (BP 10.82.30-37, the Nanda-arrival event); the eclipse gathering ends as the next event's caravan arrives.

statements.claim: The Yadavas read the eclipse not as a bad omen but as an occasion for pilgrimage; tents, campfires and an evening reunion followed.
statements.evidence: The eclipse-as-summons framing and the evening camp atmosphere (tents, news exchanged, children shown to relatives) are scene-setting connective narration; the underlying reunion of friends and kin is verse-supported.

notes: Fully grounded in BP 10.82.1-15 (+ chain to 10.82.30-37 for Nanda's arrival). 'Middle of the day', 'five pools' count, and the tented-evening scene are connective/inferential; kumkuma moved from breasts to shoulders is a modest adaptation of verse 14.

statements.claim: Nanda arrived with the cowherds, and the Vrishnis rejoiced to see him as bodies revive when life returns.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.31: 'taṃ dṛṣṭvā vṛṣṇayo hṛṣṭās tanvaḥ prāṇam ivotthitāḥ'.

statements.claim: Vasudeva was the first to reach him, embracing his old friend, pleased past words, overwhelmed with love.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.32: 'vasudevaḥ pariṣvajya samprītaḥ prema-vihvalaḥ'; verse 31 context places Vasudeva's embrace immediately on Nanda's arrival.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama came forward, bowed to Nanda and Yashoda, seated them on the seats of honor, and embraced them, speechless with love.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.33-34: 'kṛṣṇa-rāmau pariṣvajya pitarāv abhivādya ca / tāv ātmāsanam āropya bāhubhyāṃ parirabhya ca'; pack excerpt: 'speechless with love'.

statements.claim: Yashoda took her two sons onto her lap.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Yashoda takes her two sons on her lap'; BP 10.82.37 ('nyastau' — placed/resting).

statements.claim: Devaki and Rohini embraced Yashoda and spoke of the love she had shown the boys in Gokula: 'Who could forget that friendship, queen of Vraja?'
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.36: 'rohiṇī devakī cātha pariṣvajya vrajeśvarīm / kā vismareta vāṃ maitrīm anivṛttāṃ vrajeśvari'; verse 37 credits Yashoda (and Nanda) with the boys' affection, prosperity, nourishment and protection.

statements.claim: The boys, who had never known their parents' care, rested in her hands as the eyelash rests on the eye — safe and afraid of nothing.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.37: 'etāv adṛṣṭa-pitarau ... bhavati pakṣma ha yadvad akṣṇor nyastāv akutra ca bhayau'.

statements.claim: The cowherds of Gokula stood around smiling and wiping their eyes, as if they too had come home; Yashoda gave Devaki and Rohini back their sons, whole and grown.
statements.evidence: Emotional scene-setting and interpretive gloss of the embrace (verse 36-37); the mothers' mutual consolation is not spelled out in the verses but follows naturally from them.

statements.claim: Vasudeva watched from a little way off, carrying an unnameable debt he would have to speak of before the gathering ended.
statements.evidence: Internal monologue (connective narration) foreshadowing Vasudeva's confession, which the pack records in the following event (DKS_0494 / BP 10.84.58-69).

notes: Grounded in BP 10.82.30-37. Vasudeva's silent 'debt' is connective foreshadowing of his remorse speech (BP 10.84) in DKS_0494; no unsupported facts.

statements.claim: The gopis, who had not seen Krishna for a long time, came to him at Samanta-panchaka.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.38: 'gopyaś ca kṛṣṇam upalabhya cirād abhīṣṭaṃ' — obtaining Krishna, longed-for after a long time; pack index places the meeting at Samanta-panchaka.

statements.claim: They embraced him in their hearts and thereby attained a state that even the ever-yoked (nitya-yujām) can hardly reach.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.38: 'dṛgbhir hṛdī-kṛtam alaṃ parirabhya sarvās / tad-bhāvam āpur api nitya-yujāṃ durāpam'.

statements.claim: Their eyes had once cursed their own eyelids for blinking and stealing him from sight.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.38: 'yat-prekṣaṇe dṛśiṣu pakṣma-kṛtaṃ śapanti'.

statements.claim: Krishna came to them in a quiet place apart from the crowds.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.39: 'bhagavāṃs tās tathā-bhūtā vivikta upasaṅgataḥ' — the Lord approached them, thus situated, in a secluded spot.

statements.claim: He asked whether they remembered their friendship, and whether they suspected him of ingratitude.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.40-41: 'api smaratha naḥ sakhyaḥ ... / apy avadhyāyathāsmān svid akṛta-jñāviśaṅkayā'.

statements.claim: As the wind gathers clouds, grass, cotton and dust and scatters them, so the Lord brings beings together and carries them apart.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.42: 'vāyur yathā ghanānīkaṃ tṛṇaṃ tūlaṃ rajāṃsi ca'.

statements.claim: Devotion to him grants immortality to beings; he is the beginning and end of all beings, inside them and outside them.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.43-44: 'mayi bhaktir hi bhūtānām amṛtatvāya kalpate / ahaṃ hi sarva-bhūtānām ādir anto 'ntaraṃ bahiḥ'.

statements.claim: The gopis prayed that his lotus feet — contemplated in the heart by the lords of yoga, the one support for those fallen into the well of the world — would always rise in their minds, even for them who dwelt at home.
statements.evidence: BP 10.82.47: 'nalina-nābha padāravindaṃ yogeśvarair hṛdi vicintyam agādha-bodhaiḥ / saṃsāra-kūpa-patitottaraṇāvalambaṃ gehaṃ juṣām api manasy udiyāt sadā naḥ'.

statements.claim: By this instruction the gopis' bondage dissolved and they attained him.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'by which instruction the gopis, their bondage dissolved, attained him'.

statements.claim: The gopis had grown older in his absence and measured the days by his absence, counting the waiting itself as keeping him near.
statements.evidence: Interior framing of the gopis' longing (verse 38 'cirāt' supports only that much time had passed since they had seen him).

notes: Grounded in BP 10.82.38-47. The paraphrase of Krishna's teaching (wind/cloud simile, devotion as immortality, immanence) and the gopis' final prayer track the verses closely; longing-interiority is connective.

statements.claim: Nanda stayed three months, honored with great worship by the Yadavas, and the farewell lasted all that time.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Nanda stays three months, honored by the Yadavas'; BP 10.84.58: 'nandas tu saha gopālair bṛhatyā pūjayārcitaḥ'.

statements.claim: Vasudeva, weeping as he recalled the friendship, told Nanda that the snare called affection is hard to cast off, and that blinded by royal splendor he had neglected his oldest friend.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Vasudeva, weeping as he recalls the friendship, tells Nanda that the snare called affection is hard to cast off, and that blinded by royal splendor he neglected his old friend'; BP 10.84.61-62 ('prāg akalpāc ca kuśalaṃ bhrātar vo nācarāma hi').

statements.claim: In the years when it had been in his power he had done nothing for Nanda, while Nanda had done everything for his sons.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.62 + pack excerpt ('neglected his old friend, in whose house his sons grew up'); the balance of Vasudeva's debt to Nanda is the substance of the 10.84 speech as rendered in the excerpt.

statements.claim: Vasudeva said: 'May royal splendor never befall a man who desires his own good,' for it blinds the eyes.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.63: 'mā rājya-śrīr abhūt puṃsaḥ śreyas-kāmasya māna-da'; the 'steals the eyes' gloss matches the excerpt's 'blinded by royal splendor'.

statements.claim: For Vasudeva the great ocean of his longing had at last been crossed.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.59: 'vasudevo 'ñjasottīrya manoratha-mahārṇavam' — Vasudeva easily crossed the great ocean of his desire.

statements.claim: Nanda's carts were loaded with gifts from Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Krishna, Uddhava and Balarama.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.67: 'vasudevograsenābhyāṃ kṛṣṇoddhava-balādibhiḥ'; verse 66: 'kāmaiḥ pūryamāṇaḥ' (filled with objects of desire).

statements.claim: Nanda departed with the cowherds and cowherdesses of Vraja, his heart fixed on Govinda's lotus feet.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'departs with the cowherds, his heart fixed on Krishna's lotus feet'; BP 10.84.68 ('govinda-caraṇāmbuje').

statements.claim: When the kinsmen had gone, the Vrishnis, whose deity is Krishna, turned homeward.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.69: 'bandhuṣu pratiyāteṣu vṛṣṇayaḥ kṛṣṇa-devatāḥ'.

statements.claim: The caravan moved off down the road to Mathura, with Krishna walking beside Nanda's cart to the edge of the camp and Balarama and Krishna watching until the carts were small against the sky.
statements.evidence: Departure staging not verbatim in the pack (which gives no destination); Nanda's home Vraja lies in the Mathura region, and the honor Krishna/Balarama show him is verse-supported (10.84.65 'premṇā govinda-rāmayoḥ'), so this is reasonable connective narration.

statements.claim: Nanda answered Vasudeva not with a speech but with an embrace, having done what a friend does.
statements.evidence: BP 10.84.65 ('nandas tu sakhyuḥ priya-kṛt premṇā govinda-rāmayoḥ' — Nanda did what was dear to his friends through love of Govinda and Rama) supports the substance; the 'no speech' framing is connective.

notes: Grounded in BP 10.84.58-69. Note pack carries canonical event_id evt_0495 (internal id quirk; content matches the DKS_0494 farewell event). Mathura road and cart-side farewell are connective staging only.

statements.claim: Krishna delighted in Dwaraka, sporting in the lakes as the single beloved of his sixteen thousand wives.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.4-6: 'reme ṣoḍaśa-sāhasra-patnīnāṃ eka-vallabhaḥ' ... 'vijahāra vigāhyāmbho hradinīṣu mahodayaḥ'; pack index note: same scene in HV 1.235 and BP 10.90.

statements.claim: The queens surrounded him and the water-sport was mutual splashing, he sprinkling them and being sprinkled.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.8-10: 'sicyamāno 'cyutas tābhir hasantībhiḥ ... siñcan muhur yuvatibhiḥ pratiṣicyamāno'.

statements.claim: He stood among them as an elephant-lord among his cows (female elephants).
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.10: 'reme kareṇubhir ivebha-patiḥ parītaḥ'.

statements.claim: Musicians played on the bank with drums and other instruments.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.7: 'upagīyamāno gandharvair mṛdaṅga-paṇavānakān' (flutes and cymbals are connective extrapolation of the drum list).

statements.claim: Each of the sixteen thousand was certain he was sporting only with her, and there was no jealousy among them, their minds and eyes being fixed on one man.
statements.evidence: HV 1.235: 'amongst the women of Keshava every one thought: "I am the most favourite of Keshava: he is sporting only with me"'; 'those women, having their minds and eyes fixed on one man, did not cherish jealousy against one another'; BP 10.90.13 ('mukundaika-dhiyo').

statements.claim: Some queens cried out 'O Hari, I am being drowned — save me!' and clung to him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.235: 'Some of them, having eyes like a deer, held Hari by the neck, and said: "O Hari, I am being drowned, save me"'.

statements.claim: Some rowed small boats shaped like herons, serpents and sea-monsters; some swam by their own strength and some with water jars.
statements.evidence: HV 1.235: 'began to row in wooden boats of the shape of herons and serpents ... Makara-shaped boats'; 'some swam depending on their own breast and some on water jars'.

statements.claim: The water stood at the knee of one, the thigh of another, the breast of a third, each met exactly as she came.
statements.evidence: HV 1.235: 'The ocean yielded its water to whatever extent the women wanted, either up to their knees, thighs or breast' (rendered here as playful water in the Dwaraka lakes, per the pack's treatment of BP 10.90 + HV 1.235 as the same scene).

statements.claim: His garland was streaked with saffron and his hair fell loose about his face from the play.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.10: 'tat-stana-viṣajjita-kuṅkuma-srak / krīḍābhiṣaṅga-dhuta-kuntala-vṛnda-bandhaḥ'.

statements.claim: The queens sang songs of longing to the osprey, the shelduck, the waning moon, the southern breeze, the rain-clouds and a swan, asking it of Shauri the Unconquered One and of his fickle friendship.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.14-23: songs to the kurari (v.14), cakravākī (v.15), moon (v.17), malayānila/southern breeze (v.18), megha/clouds (v.19), and the haṃsa/swan (v.23: 'haṃsa svāgatam ... brūhy aṅga śaureḥ kathāṃ ... kaccid ajitaḥ svasty āsta ... kiṃ vā naś cala-sauhṛdaḥ smarati').

statements.claim: By such constant, single-hearted love the queens attained the supreme state.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'by such constant love attain the supreme state' (BP 10.90 context).

statements.claim: The city had settled back into pleasure after the long years of exile and war, with elephants in the streets, heavy gardens and music.
statements.evidence: BP 10.90.1-3 describes the flower-laden, elephant-thronged city; the 'after exile and war' timeline and 'music never quite stopped' are connective framing.

notes: Grounded in BP 10.90.1-24 + HV 1.235 (pack treats both as the same water-sport scene, each-queen-believes-she-is-favoured motif). Water-at-knee/thigh/breast and boats come from HV; songs from BP.

statements.claim: King Dhritarashtra, whose hundred sons had been slain, set out from Hastinapura (the city called after the elephant) in grief to meet the Pandavas.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12 (Ganguli): 'king Yudhishthira the just heard that his uncle Dhritarashtra had set out from the city called after the elephant. Afflicted with grief on account of the death of his sons.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira went out to meet him with his brothers, Krishna of Dasharha's race, Yuyudhana and Yuyutsu; Draupadi, burning with grief, followed her lord.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'The son of Kunti was followed by the high-souled and heroic Krishna of Dasharha's race, and by Yuyudhana, as also by Yuyutsu. The princess Draupadi also, burning with grief ... sorrowfully followed her lord.'

statements.claim: On the banks of the Ganga the Bharata ladies wept like a flight of ospreys, arms raised, asking where was the righteousness of the king who had slain sires, brothers, preceptors, sons and friends.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'the crowd of Bharata ladies afflicted with woe and crying like a flight of she-ospreys ... with arms raised aloft in grief ... "Where, indeed, is that righteousness of the king ... since he has slain sires and brothers and preceptors and sons and friends?"'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira saluted his uncle's feet and the brothers announced themselves, each giving his own name.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'Yudhishthira the just saluted the feet of his eldest uncle. Having saluted their sire according to custom ... the Pandavas, announced themselves to him, each uttering his own name.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra reluctantly embraced Yudhishthira with a few words of comfort, then sought Bhima, his wrath a fire fanned by the wind of grief, ready to consume the Bhima-forest.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'reluctantly embraced the eldest son of Pandu ... Having embraced Yudhishthira the just and spoken a few words of comfort ... the wicked-souled Dhritarashtra sought for Bhima, like a blazing fire ... that fire of his wrath, fanned by the wind of his grief, seemed then to be ready to consume the Bhima-forest.'

statements.claim: Krishna, who had understood Dhritarashtra's intentions from the very outset and kept ready an iron statue of Bhima made at Duryodhana's order, drew the real Bhima away and set the statue in the king's embrace.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'Ascertaining the evil intentions cherished by him towards Bhima, Krishna, dragging away the real Bhima, presented an iron statue of the second son of Pandu to the old king. Possessed of great intelligence, Krishna had, at the very outset, understood the intentions ... and had, therefore, kept such a contrivance ready' ... 'that iron statue of Bhima, which had been caused to be made by thy son, had been kept ready for thee.'

statements.claim: The blind king, endued with the strength of ten thousand elephants, crushed the iron statue as if it were a reed; his own breast was bruised, he vomited blood and fell like a parijata tree topped with its flowery burden.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'Endued with might equal to that of 10,000 elephants, the king reduced that statue into fragments. His own breast, however, became considerably bruised and he began to vomit blood. Covered with blood, the king fell down on the ground like a parijata tree topped with its flowery burden.'

statements.claim: Sanjaya, son of Gavalgana, raised and steadied him, saying 'Do not act so,' and the king, his wrath spent, wept 'Alas, oh Bhima, alas, oh Bhima!'
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: 'His learned charioteer Sanjaya, the son of Gavalgana, raised the monarch and soothing and comforting him, said, "Do not act so." The king then ... began to weep aloud, saying, "Alas, oh Bhima, alas, oh Bhima!"'

statements.claim: Krishna revealed that the king had broken only an iron statue, that no one can escape the pressure of his arms as no one escapes the Destroyer, and that the slaughter of Bhima would not revive his sons — bidding him approve what was done for peace and not set his heart on grief.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.12: Krishna's speech — 'Do not grieve, O Dhritarashtra, for thou hast not slain Bhimasena! That is an iron statue ... there is none equal to thee in strength of body ... as no one can escape with life from an encounter with the Destroyer himself, even so no body can come out safe from within thy embrace ... The slaughter of Bhima ... would do thee no good. Thy sons ... would not be revived by it. Therefore, do thou approve of what has been by us with a view to secure peace and do not set thy heart on grief!'

statements.claim: The whole court watched the approach with dread no one spoke aloud, and the meeting 'should have been a simple one — a nephew comforting an uncle'.
statements.evidence: Connective tension-building framing around the supported events (the king's murderous intent is itself verse-supported).

notes: Very close rendering of MBh 11.12 (Ganguli), including the iron statue, the 10,000-elephant strength, and Krishna's full speech. 'He wanted the man who had killed Duryodhana' relies on the war-arc canon that Bhima slew Duryodhana (corpus chain).

statements.claim: Maid-servants came and washed the king after he had been bloodied, and then Krishna addressed him again.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'Certain maid-servants then came to the king for washing him. After he had been duly washed, the slayer of Madhu again addressed him.' ('Dressed his wounds' is a small connective extension of the washing scene.)

statements.claim: Krishna told the king he had read the Vedas and scriptures, heard the old histories and everything about the duties of kings, and was learned, wise and indifferent to strength and weakness — so why cherish wrath when all that overtook him was his own fault?
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'Thou hast, O king, read the Vedas and diverse scriptures. Thou hast heard all old histories, and everything about the duties of kings. Thou art learned, possessed of great wisdom, and indifferent to strength and weakness. Why then dost thou cherish such wrath when all that has overtaken thee is the result of thy own fault?'

statements.claim: Krishna, Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and Sanjaya had counselled him before the war, telling him the Pandavas were superior to his sons in strength and courage, but he had not followed their advice.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'I spoke to thee before the battle. Both Bhishma and Drona ... did the same, as also Vidura and Sanjaya. Thou didst not, however, then follow our advice ... knowing that the Pandavas were superior to thee and thine ... in strength and courage.'

statements.claim: A king who can see his own faults and knows the distinctions of place and time obtains great prosperity; one who rejects the counsel of well-wishers meets distress and grieves over the policy he chose.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'That king who is capable of seeing his own faults and knows the distinctions of place and time, obtains great prosperity. That person, however, who, though counselled by well-wishers, does not accept their words, good or bad, meets with distress and is obliged to grieve in consequence of the evil policy he pursues.'

statements.claim: The king had not kept his soul under restraint but let Duryodhana rule him; Krishna urged him to observe a different course, recollect his own faults and govern his wrath.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'Thou didst not keep thy soul under restraint, but suffered thyself to be ruled by Duryodhana. That which has come upon thee is due to thy own fault. Why then dost thou seek to slay Bhima? Recollecting thy own faults, govern thy wrath now.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana had, from pride, caused the princess of Pancala to be brought into the assembly, and that mean wretch had been slain by Bhimasena in just revenge.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'That mean wretch who had, from pride, caused the princess of Pancala to be brought into the assembly has been slain by Bhimasena in just revenge.'

statements.claim: Krishna declared the sons of Pandu perfectly innocent yet treated most cruelly by the king and his son.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'The sons of Pandu are perfectly innocent. Yet have they been treated most cruelly by thee and him.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra acknowledged it was parental affection for his own sons that made him fall away from righteousness, that by good luck Bhima had never come within his embrace, and that, free of wrath and fever, he now desired to embrace Bhima, on the Pandavas depending his welfare and happiness.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'It is parental affection ... that caused me to fall away from righteousness ... By good luck, that tiger among men, the mighty Bhima of true prowess, protected by thee, came not within my embrace. Now, however, I am free from wrath and fever. I desire eagerly ... to embrace that hero ... When all the kings have been dead, when my children are no more, upon the sons of Pandu depend my welfare and happiness.'

statements.claim: The old king then embraced Bhima, Dhananjaya and the two sons of Madri, weeping over them, comforting them and pronouncing blessings upon them.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.13: 'the old king then embraced those princes of excellent frames, Bhima and Dhananjaya, and those two foremost of men, the two sons of Madri, and wept, and comforted and pronounced blessings upon them.'

statements.claim: An hour earlier he had crushed what he believed was Bhima in his arms — an iron statue Krishna had substituted.
statements.evidence: Recap of the immediately preceding canonical event, supported by MBh 11.12 in the DKS_0496 pack ('Krishna ... presented an iron statue of the second son of Pandu to the old king'); 'an hour earlier' is connective timing.

notes: Faithful rendering of MBh 11.13 (Ganguli); Krishna's admonition and Dhritarashtra's reply track the passage nearly sentence by sentence. 'Dressed his wounds' is a mild extension of the washing scene.

statements.claim: Gandhari had just cursed Krishna — that he would die, as her sons had died, by the hands of his own kinsmen — and he had accepted the curse with a smile.
statements.evidence: Continuity with the immediately preceding canonical event (corpus-chain previous story DKS_0498, 'Gandhari Curses Krishna; He Accepts with a Smile'); the MBh 11.26 passage has Krishna answer Gandhari's grief right after the curse.

statements.claim: Krishna told Gandhari to arise and not set her heart on grief, for through her own fault the vast carnage had taken place.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Arise, arise, O Gandhari, do not set thy heart on grief! Through thy fault, this vast carnage has taken place!'

statements.claim: Duryodhana was wicked-souled, envious and exceedingly arrogant; Gandhari applauded his wicked acts and regarded them as good; he was cruel, the embodiment of hostilities, and disobedient to the counsel of the elders.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Thy son Duryodhana was wicked-souled, envious, and exceedingly arrogant. Applauding his wicked acts, thou regardest them to be good. Exceedingly cruel, he was the embodiment of hostilities, and disobedient to the injunctions of the old.'

statements.claim: Krishna asked Gandhari why she wished to ascribe her own faults to him.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Why dost thou wish to ascribe thy own faults to me?'

statements.claim: One who grieves for what has already occurred obtains more grief; by indulging in grief one increases it two-fold.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Dead or lost, the person that grieves for what has already occurred, obtaineth more grief. By indulging in grief, one increases it two-fold.'

statements.claim: The woman of the priestly class bears sons for austerities, the cow for burdens, the mare for speed, the servant-woman for servitors, the herdsman's wife for keepers of cattle — but a princess bears sons for being slaughtered.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'A woman of the regenerate class bears children for the practice of austerities; the cow brings forth offspring for bearing burdens; the mare brings forth her young for acquiring speed of motion; the Shudra woman bears a child for adding to the number of servitors; the Vaishya woman for adding to the number of keepers of cattle. A princess, however, like thee, brings forth sons for being slaughtered!'

statements.claim: Gandhari remained silent, her heart exceedingly agitated by grief.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Gandhari, with heart exceedingly agitated by grief, remained silent.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra asked Yudhishthira how many had fallen and how many had escaped; Yudhishthira answered one billion, six hundred and sixty million and twenty thousand fallen, and two hundred and forty thousand one hundred and sixty-five escaped.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'One billion 660 million and 20,000 men have fallen in this battle. Of the heroes that have escaped, the number is 240,165.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira told where the fallen had gone: those who cast off their bodies gladly in fierce battle reached regions like Indra's; those who died without joy found the company of the celestial musicians (Gandharvas); those who fell turning away or begging quarter reached the world of the hidden ones (guhyakas); the high-souled who advanced unarmed against armed foes attained the bright regions of Brahman; the rest attained the region of the Uttara-Kurus.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Those warriors of true prowess that have cheerfully cast off their bodies in fierce battle have all attained regions like those of Indra ... they that have encountered it cheerlessly have attained the companionship of the Gandharvas. Those warriors that have fallen ... while turning away from the field or begging for quarter, have attained the world of the guhyakas. Those high-souled warriors ... advancing unarmed against fighting foes, have all assumed bright forms and attained the regions of Brahman. The remaining warriors ... have attained the region of the Uttara-Kurus.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira had received the gift of spiritual sight from the sage Lomasa during his years of wandering.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'While at thy command I wandered in the forest, I obtained this boon ... I met with the celestial rishi Lomasa and obtained from him the boon of spiritual vision.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira commanded that the funeral rites of the slain be duly performed so that nobody might perish for want of someone to care for them.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'Cause the funeral rites of the slain, numbering by thousands, to be duly performed, so that nobody may perish for want of persons to take care of them!'

statements.claim: Pyres were built of sandalwood, aloe and gathered wood, with ghee, oil, perfumes, silken robes, broken chariots and heaps of weapons, and were lit; Duryodhana and his hundred brothers, Shalya, Jayadratha, Abhimanyu, Duhshasana's son, Bhurishrava, Drupada, Virata, Shikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna and the thousands of Srinjayas were burned with due rites.
statements.evidence: MBh 11.26: 'procuring sandal, aloe and other kinds of wood ... clarified butter and oil and perfumes and costly silken robes ... large heaps of dry wood, and broken cars and diverse kinds of weapons, caused funeral pyres to be duly made and lighted and then without haste burnt, with due rites the slain kings ... the bodies of Duryodhana and his hundred brothers, of Shalya, and king Bhurishrava; of king Jayadratha and Abhimanyu ... of Duhshasana's son ... of Virata and Drupada; of Shikhandi ... and Dhrishtadyumna ... and the hundreds of Srinjayas.'

statements.claim: Krishna spoke 'with the pyres not yet built', and Dhritarashtra had been listening at Gandhari's side.
statements.evidence: Timing/staging connective narration; the passage order (rebuke, numbers, then the funeral command) supports the sequence, and Dhritarashtra's presence is implied by his immediately following question.

notes: Faithful rendering of MBh 11.26 (Ganguli) — the rebuke, the grief teaching, the classes of women, the casualty numbers (1,660,020,000 fallen; 240,165 escaped), the ends of the fallen, and the funeral of the named kings all track the passage. Curse recap relies on chain continuity with DKS_0498.
